results.title: The aesthetics of comparativeness in Clifford Geertz's Islam Observed
results.content: In *Islam Observed*: *Religious Development in Morocco and Indonesia*, the anthropologist Clifford Geertz demonstrated the extent to which cultural anthropology can recount and revisit social formulations of religions and thus reopen new horizons and positionalities in understanding and perceiving religion practices by employing a comparative methodology that combines disciplines of anthropology, ethnography, sociology, and literature. In fact, the very focus of modern anthropology of culture—with Clifford Geertz as one of its pioneering scholars—is the ‘socially available systems of significance’ (Geertz 1968 Islam observed: religious development in Morocco and Indonesia. In *Islam Observed*, Clifford Geertz asks: “Is the comparative study of religion condemned to mindless description and an equally mindless celebration of the unique?” (Geertz 1968 Islam observed: religious development in Morocco and Indonesia. Widely recognised as a key contributor to both anthropology and the study of Islam, Clifford Geertz’s theory of cultural systems centres on the pivotal role of socio-linguistic structures and symbolic systems in shaping anthropological discourse.

Menchaca is an Assistant Professor of History at the University of Southern California where she specializes in nineteenth century U.S-Mexico borderlands history. She was previously Assistant Professor of Early American History at California State University San Marcos, and a Postdoctoral Fellow in History and Digital Humanities at the University of Southern California. Liza Blake is an Associate Professor of English at the University of Toronto, with research interests in early modern literature, science, and philosophy; early modern women’s writing; book history; textual editing; and asexuality studies.
